style.a: Idempotency means that sending the same request many times produces the same final state as sending it once, so retries do not create duplicate records. It is a property of the operation, not of the HTTP method: GET and PUT are idempotent by design, while POST is not, because each request creates a new resource. Idempotency protects against transient failures and retries, but it does not make a request atomic or safe against concurrent updates.

Python threads share the interpreter and its global state, so they cannot run C extensions written in CPython bytecode in parallel. The GIL serializes bytecode execution, and many built-in operations acquire it. Multiprocessing spawns separate processes, each with its own interpreter and memory, so CPU-bound work can use multiple cores. The cost is interprocess communication and serialization, and pickling objects to share data. For I/O-bound work, threads or asyncio are often preferable.
